title: Cephalonauts One: A deep fMRI dataset for decoding naturalistic speech in the human brain
claim: A dataset is defined by its acquisition setup and repeated session structure, showing how stimulus and brain recordings are paired.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; A scanner and aligned time series, B session timeline
description: Two panels labeled A and B. Panel A, 'Acquisition setup', shows a line-drawn MRI scanner with a person lying inside. Beside it are scan parameters (3T MRI, 2D EPI SMS 6, TR ~2 Hz). Below is a time axis from 0 to 1 s with a shaded 'Frame' column. Under the axis are three grayscale brain images labeled X, then an audio waveform labeled Z, then the French transcript 'Ce sont des très grands modèles…'. Panel B, 'Session setup', shows a dashed box for a ~1.5 hour session. It contains five green-to-teal squares for ~15 min runs, each followed by a triangle for questions, and a gray circle for the T1 anatomical scan. Green bars group the runs under Podcast 1, 2 and 3. A time axis runs from 0 to 3600 s. Multipliers x24 sessions and x3 subjects sit to the right, and a legend is at the bottom. The eye goes first to the scanner and the green run blocks.
caption: Overview of the \dataset dataset. A. Three subjects listened to podcasts during fMRI acquisition. B. Each session included five 15-minute runs, three comprehension questions after each run, and a final anatomical scan. Runs 1--2, 3--4, and 5 used three distinct podcasts and podcasts were not repeated across sessions.
abstract: Cephalonauts One is a whole-brain 3 Tesla (3T) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) dataset recorded while subjects listened to audio podcasts. Three healthy subjects underwent multiple scanning sessions, each consisting of five 15-minute runs, while listening to podcasts in their native language. With 30 hours of fMRI data per subject, the current release is the deepest available fMRI dataset using naturalistic speech stimuli. The dataset pairs brain activity with the corresponding podcast audio, transcript annotations, and derived stimulus embeddings. Furthermore, we introduce a brain decoding benchmark formulated as audio segment retrieval: given fMRI activity from a held-out session, the decoder must identify the corresponding time-aligned podcast audio segment among candidate segments. We provide standardized splits, evaluation metrics, and baseline decoders for this task. Finally, a scaling analysis shows that decoding performance improves continuously with the amount of training data per subject.
